papers.title: Judicial Review of EU acts
papers.summary: Judicial review is the cornerstone for any society that can be considered truly democratic. The process of judicial review enables the courts to scrutinise the legality of administrative and legislative acts. Within the EU legal framework, Article 263 TFEU provides for the primary mechanism for this judicial oversight. Article 263 TFEU allows for direct challenges to the legality of EU measures, focusing on four key elements: the types of reviewable acts, eligible applicants, time limitations, and grounds for review. A complete system of judicial review requires not only that Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies act lawfully, but also that they act when they have a duty to do so. The chapter focuses on the extent to which non-privileged applicants are adequately protected by the Union legal order, in particular as regards the rules relating to locus standi and -consequently- the right of access to a court.

papers.summary: This project tests a model of cooperation in which breaking an explicit cooperative promise (“defection”) carries a cognitive cost, and individuals anticipate and manage that cost when deciding how to act. The key manipulation is the size of a bonus for a second memory test offered later in the study ($1 vs $20). papers.title: The Transformative Potential of the Beauty Industry: From Visual Aesthetics to the Psychological Restoration of the Individual
papers.summary: The beauty industry is evolving from a focus on visual enhancement toward a multidimensional system that supports psychological restoration and identity formation. The aim of this study is to analyze the transformative potential of aesthetic practices in improving individual well-being. Methods include a systematic review of recent interdisciplinary studies and comparative analysis of aesthetic and psycho-emotional outcomes. Results indicate that modern beauty practices—such as skincare programs, makeup, and hairstyling—significantly influence self-esteem, emotional stability, and social integration. Furthermore, the integration of digital technologies and personalized approaches enhances these effects. The findings confirm that the beauty industry functions not only as a commercial sector but also as a socio-cultural and therapeutic mechanism, contributing to holistic personal development and psychological resilience in contemporary society.

papers.summary: The beauty industry is evolving from a focus on visual enhancement toward a multidimensional system that supports psychological restoration and identity formation. The aim of this study is to analyze the transformative potential of aesthetic practices in improving individual well-being. Methods include a systematic review of recent interdisciplinary studies and comparative analysis of aesthetic and psycho-emotional outcomes. Results indicate that modern beauty practices—such as skincare programs, makeup, and hairstyling—significantly influence self-esteem, emotional stability, and social integration. Furthermore, the integration of digital technologies and personalized approaches enhances these effects. The findings confirm that the beauty industry functions not only as a commercial sector but also as a socio-cultural and therapeutic mechanism, contributing to holistic personal development and psychological resilience in contemporary society.

papers.summary: The thesis examines how self-censorship manifests in Saudi cinema and how it defines on-screen representations and aesthetics. Conventional studies on film censorship have typically adopted a binary framework, positioning filmmakers in opposition to institutional censorship. papers.title: Experiencing Shakespeare's Theatres:Playgoing, Pleasure and Judgement in Early Modern England
papers.summary: In this transformative study, Simon Smith explores how playwrights like Shakespeare crafted their plays for demanding and varied commercial audiences. Rediscovering the many forms of judgement practiced in the early modern playhouse, he investigates influences ranging from the classical tradition and grammar-school classroom to ballad and jest culture. Where many prior studies have treated 'the judicious' as a self-contained subset of playgoers, Smith reveals the variety of careful assessments made in the theatre by a wide range of playgoers, showing that judgement and pleasure were often simultaneous elements of the same response. Chapters examine specific parts of plays that were especially subject to evaluation and generative of enjoyment: spectacle, words, plot, and actorly technique. Close readings shed fresh light on much-studied plays like Hamlet and Volpone, as well as exploring several unfairly overlooked plays.
